Brand Positioning Using Multidimensional Scaling Technique (https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/0972262919850930)
# Brand Positioning Using Multidimensional Scaling Technique: An Application to Herbal Healthcare Brands in Indian Market

Vision The Journal of Business Perspective. Published: 2019-08-04. 10 citations.

## Abstract

The purpose of this article is to identify significant differences in the positioning of brands in the segment of herbal healthcare in Indian market by multidimensional scaling (MDS) method. The herbal healthcare market is an ever-growing segment of the healthcare market, due to the increasing trend towards self-medication and inclination to the use of natural products. The research presents insights into the importance of marketing attributes which influence the consumer perception of this segment. The study was conducted in North India using a structured questionnaire with a five-point Likert scale. A derived approach to MDS was used in which consumer perception ratings of selected brands on various marketing attributes were done. These nine attributes were identified and itemized from the review of literature and pre-tests as per their importance to consumer. Factor analysis deduced important marketing dimensions from these nine attributes namely product quality (PQ), brand effect (BE) and price affordability (PA). MDS was used to map the perception of selected brands, drawing two-dimensional maps. The brands selected were on the basis of a pre-test which identified the most commonly used brands in the segment as Dabur, Himalaya, Zandu, Patanjali and Hamdard. The results indicate that Dabur and Himalaya are positioned higher than Zandu, Patanjali and Hamdard in the minds of the consumers on quality and BE, with both occupying a strong positive quality and brand image perception. Hamdard had a high BE, but low-quality perception, and Zandu reported a near neutral perception on all the marketing dimensions. Patanjali has a higher PA perception in comparison to the other brands, however, the segment of herbal healthcare was found to be price tolerant. Finally, the article presents conclusions and important managerial implications with the scope of further research and directions.

Zandu's Ayurvedic Brand Strategy in Healthcare (https://www.markhub24.com/post/zandu-s-ayurvedic-brand-strategy-in-healthcare)
Zandu's Ayurvedic Brand Strategy in Healthcare

# Zandu's Ayurvedic Brand Strategy in Healthcare

Jun 22 10 min read

## Industry & Competitive Context

The Indian Ayurvedic and herbal healthcare market represents one of the most strategically complex battlegrounds in the country's FMCG landscape. Emami, which owns Zandu Ayurveda and has a portfolio of over 300 products based on Ayurvedic formulations across its brands, has publicly stated its conviction that "Ayurveda will continue to be more relevant." This conviction sits within a category that has been transformed since the mid-2010s by two structural disruptions: the rise of Patanjali Ayurved as a mass-market disruptor backed by cultural nationalism, and the post-COVID immunity wave that sharply elevated consumer willingness to pay for Ayurvedic wellness products. The competitive landscape in Ayurvedic OTC healthcare includes Dabur (with Chyawanprash, Honey, and Hajmola), Himalaya Drug Company, Baidyanath, and newer digital-first challengers such as The Ayurveda Co. and Kapiva. Each of these brands operates on a different axis — Dabur on mass scale, Himalaya on clinical credibility, and Patanjali on price-value and cultural resonance. Zandu's challenge, and opportunity, has been to leverage over a century of institutional heritage while simultaneously competing in modern channels against digitally agile entrants.

Expand image

## Brand Situation Prior to Strategy Shift

Zandu Pharmaceutical Works Limited was founded in 1910, rooted in a lineage of classical Ayurvedic practice. The brand was established with a focus on Ayurvedic expertise developed over more than a century, carrying strong brand trust and recall through products including Zandu Balm, Zandu Chyawanprash, Zandu Pancharishta, and Zandu Kesari Jivan. For most of its independent existence, Zandu operated as a pharmaceuticals-oriented Ayurvedic company with limited investment in modern marketing infrastructure. In May 2008, Emami acquired a 27.51% stake in Zandu Pharmaceutical Works Ltd. from co-promoters for ₹170 crore via an off-market transaction, followed by an open offer for additional shares. By October 2008, Emami completed the full acquisition of Zandu for approximately ₹750 crore. At the point of acquisition, Zandu was primarily a legacy pharmaceutical business with deep product heritage but limited FMCG-grade distribution, communication architecture, or modern brand management. The acquisition price — significant for its time — reflected the strategic premium Emami placed on Zandu's brand equity, particularly the century-old institutional authority in Ayurvedic healthcare. The pre-acquisition Emami was a mid-sized personal care FMCG player with strong regional recognition and high advertising intensity, maintaining A&P-to-sales ratios of 16–18% among the highest in Indian FMCG. However, it lacked the institutional Ayurvedic healthcare credibility that legacy brands like Zandu — founded in 1910 by physician lineage — carried in the Indian consumer's mind. This gap between Emami's consumer reach and Zandu's healthcare authority defined the strategic logic of the integration.

## Strategic Objective

Emami's documented strategic intent for Zandu has operated at two distinct levels across two phases. In the first phase (2008–2019), the objective was integration and growth: to transition Zandu from a pharmaceuticals business into an FMCG-model Ayurvedic healthcare brand, while leveraging Emami's distribution reach and advertising firepower. In the second phase (2020 onwards), the objective shifted toward platform building: to establish Zandu as a full-spectrum Ayurvedic wellness brand operating across traditional trade, modern trade, and digital direct-to-consumer channels. As stated in Emami's Annual Report for 2013–14, Managing Director Sushil K. Goenka articulated the brand's direction: "We aim to grow our healthcare portfolio of OTC and generic products under the Zandu umbrella. We are optimistic about the OTC healthcare market in India which is growing at 25–30% annually." This public declaration of intent — to position Zandu as the organizing umbrella for Emami's entire healthcare ambition — was a foundational strategic choice with long-term brand architecture implications. The objective was not merely to grow Zandu's revenue, but to use the brand's heritage credibility as a trust anchor for portfolio expansion into adjacent OTC categories including digestive health, immunity, energy, and pain management.

## Positioning & Consumer Insight

Zandu's positioning rests on a deep structural insight about how Indian consumers relate to health: that Ayurvedic remedies occupy a distinct mental space that bridges preventive care and therapeutic relief, without requiring the clinical credibility demanded of allopathic products. Emami has positioned Zandu as a brand that provides "pure and effective 'guaranteed 100% vegetarian' products of superior quality," with the claim that Zandu products "carry the hallmark of the 5000-year-old science of Ayurveda, and work best as prevention-oriented solutions that help in disease management." This positioning constructs three consumer-relevant equities simultaneously: purity (no non-vegetarian ingredients), efficacy (rooted in ancient science), and safety (natural formulations). In the Indian consumer's decision-making framework for self-medication and wellness supplementation, these equities collectively address what is best understood through the Jobs-to-Be-Done lens as the "trusted family healthcare guardian" job — a role that neither modern pharmaceutical brands nor generic Ayurvedic manufacturers can easily claim. The pain management segment illustrates this positioning most sharply. Zandu Balm is described as "India's No. 1 pain relieving balm," available in more than 5 crore Indian households across geographies, and is considered by many consumers to be a generic name for balms — synonymous with headache, body ache, and cold remedy. Generic-brand status — where a brand name becomes a category descriptor — represents the highest form of mental availability in brand strategy. Zandu Balm's achievement of this status is the result of decades of consistent formulation and category association, not a manufactured positioning exercise. Emami's core positioning insight rests on a deep understanding of how Indian middle-class consumers — particularly in semi-urban and rural markets — relate to health and personal care not as entirely separate domains, but as a continuum of wellbeing. The Indian consumer has historically used the same Ayurvedic formulation logic for both skin protection and pain relief. Zandu's brand architecture exploits this continuum by extending from balm (pain management) to Pancharishta (digestive health) to Chyawanprash (immunity) to Kesari Jivan (vitality), creating a portfolio that serves a consumer across the full arc of daily health management.

## Campaign Architecture & Execution

Emami's brand-building strategy for Zandu has followed a two-track architecture. The first track is rooted in traditional FMCG tools: celebrity endorsement, mass media communication, and packaging renovation. Emami engaged an international consultant to reinforce communication and brand architecture of Zandu, and stated its intent to invest aggressively in brand spending through celebrity endorsements. This investment in above-the-line communication was essential to migrate Zandu from a pharmacy-counter brand to a household FMCG brand with modern salience. The second track — significantly more strategically differentiated — involves the construction of a D2C digital platform purpose-built for the healthcare brand. Emami launched its own e-portal ZanduCare.com, through which the company launched digital-first innovative products under the Zandu Healthcare umbrella in the categories of immunity and wellness, with management noting that "launch of digital first brands is the next big shift in consumer offering that will drive the growth trajectory of the FMCG sector." The ZanduCare platform is not merely an e-commerce channel — it serves as a product development sandbox. Emami launched more than 20 healthcare products under the ZanduCare D2C platform in FY22 alone. This approach — testing and commercializing new product concepts exclusively through D2C before broader rollout — represents a modern innovation architecture that legacy Ayurvedic brands have rarely employed with this level of discipline. The product range extension strategy has been equally deliberate. Post-acquisition, Emami systematically grew the Zandu portfolio from its core incumbents (Balm, Pancharishta, Chyawanprash, Kesari Jivan) into new sub-segments, including Zandu Nityam for constipation management, Zandu Vigorex for male vitality, immunity products such as Zandu Immu Jelly for children, and Zandu Tulsi Drops for respiratory health during COVID-19. Each launch was designed to extend the brand's authority into adjacent healthcare territories without departing from the Ayurvedic formulation logic that forms Zandu's core credibility.

## Media & Channel Strategy

Emami's channel strategy for Zandu has evolved across three distinct phases, each corresponding to a shift in distribution economics and consumer behavior. In Phase One (2008–2015), the priority was general trade penetration — distributing Zandu's OTC products through Emami's existing trade infrastructure to unlock geographic scale. The Zandu portfolio contributed ₹400 crore and accounted for 22% of Emami's total turnover of ₹1,821 crore in FY14, with the healthcare business growing 36% in that year. In Phase Two (2015–2020), Emami layered modern trade and institutional channels onto the general trade base. The company's investment in brand communication for key Zandu SKUs — particularly Pancharishta and Balm — sought to build national salience that would support modern trade listings and drive category premiumization. Phase Three (post-2020) is defined by the D2C and digital-first strategy. Emami launched D2C websites for Zandu, Kesh King, and BoroPlus. Its e-commerce revenues doubled and contributed 5.5% to its domestic business in FY22, up from 2.8% in the previous year. The ZanduCare platform specifically serves as the innovation and margin-accretive channel for the healthcare brand, enabling product launches with higher price points targeting urban, health-conscious, digitally active consumers — a segment structurally different from Zandu's traditional rural mass-market consumer base. By FY25, organised trade channels comprising modern trade, e-commerce, and institutional sales contributed 27.6% of domestic revenues, expanding by 140 basis points year-on-year, and clocking 13% growth — outpacing overall domestic growth. This data reflects a structural channel shift that Zandu, as the flagship healthcare brand, has been central to driving.

## Business & Brand Outcomes

At the acquisition level, Emami paid approximately ₹730–750 crore for Zandu in 2008. Emami subsequently became debt-free within two years of the deal, indicating exceptional cash generation post-integration. This financial recovery speed is a documented indicator of operational synergy realization between the two entities. At the revenue level, the Zandu portfolio's trajectory is traceable through Emami's public filings. From ₹400 crore in FY14 representing 22% of Emami's then-turnover, the healthcare portfolio — anchored by Zandu — has grown substantially. In FY25, Emami's healthcare portfolio grew 13% year-on-year, led by the D2C portfolio ZanduCare, which recorded growth of nearly 50%, driven by new product launches and marketing initiatives. At the digital channel level, the ZanduCare strategy has achieved measurable scale. ZanduCare's digital-first portfolio now contributes over 80% of ZanduCare's total sales, with 11 of the FY25 new product launches introduced exclusively on the D2C platform. At the brand portfolio level, the overall contribution of acquired brands — of which Zandu is the largest — has grown significantly. Sales from acquired brands rose from 15% of total Emami revenue in FY20 to 33% in FY25. In the pain management segment specifically, Emami noted that Zandu Ultra Power and Menthol Pain Balm saw healthy growth, though the mother brand Zandu Green Balm remained under pressure, with the company relying on new product launches to sustain the segment. This observation is analytically significant — it signals that while the extended Zandu portfolio is gaining ground, the core heritage SKU is facing competitive pressure, likely from lower-priced competitors in the balm category. Emami's domestic revenue reached ₹3,159 crore in FY25, reflecting 6.8% year-over-year growth, with Zandu, Navratna, and BoroPlus named as the core brand anchors of this performance.

## Strategic Implications

1. Heritage as a Strategic Asset, Not a Legacy Burden. Zandu's most durable competitive advantage is its institutional authority in Ayurvedic healthcare — the product of over a century of consistent formulation and consumer trust-building. Emami's key strategic insight was that this heritage could be transferred and amplified within an FMCG operating model, rather than preserved within a pharmaceutical business structure. The 2008 acquisition was not merely a revenue consolidation exercise; it was a brand equity acquisition that enabled Emami to enter the Ayurvedic healthcare trust space from which its personal care brands were excluded.

2. Portfolio Breadth as Category Defense. Zandu's expansion from a single iconic SKU (Balm) to a multi-category healthcare portfolio covering pain, digestion, immunity, vitality, and cough management reflects a deliberate category-locking strategy. By owning multiple high-salience Ayurvedic OTC formulations under one brand umbrella, Emami reduces the vulnerability of any single SKU to competitive displacement, while simultaneously making Zandu a more powerful retail shelf negotiator. This is a documented portfolio management principle — breadth creates resistance to point-of-sale substitution.

3. D2C as Innovation Infrastructure, Not Just Revenue Channel. The ZanduCare platform's most strategically significant function is not revenue generation per se, but the ability to test, learn, and launch new Ayurvedic wellness products with lower capital commitment and faster consumer feedback loops. The documented pattern of launching products exclusively on ZanduCare before broader rollout indicates that Emami has constructed a product innovation pipeline that runs through its digital channel — a structural capability that traditional trade brands cannot easily replicate.

4. The Demographic Bridge Problem. Zandu's core consumer — urban-rural middle-class, 35+, using Ayurvedic OTC products for chronic condition management — is increasingly aging. The post-COVID immunity wave attracted younger consumers to the Ayurvedic wellness category, but retaining these consumers requires different brand communication, product formats, and channel strategies than those used for Zandu's traditional base. The documented pressure on the mother Zandu Balm brand, alongside the strong performance of ZanduCare's digital-first portfolio, reflects this transition challenge: the heritage brand may be losing salience among younger consumers even as extended portfolio innovations attract them.

5. Competitive Moat vs. Commodity Risk. The Ayurvedic OTC space in India faces structural commoditization risk — formulations are not proprietary, heritage claims are widely made, and Patanjali's entry demonstrated that price disruption is possible at scale. Zandu's sustainable competitive moat lies not in its formulations but in its mental availability, distribution depth, and the institutional trust that over a century of consistent market presence has built. Maintaining this moat requires continuous investment in both brand communication and quality consistency — both of which are documented priorities in Emami's public management commentary.
